name: Carla Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four and at the Brookfield Wholesale depot by quarter to six. I drive a twelve-tonne rigid, loaded with crates of milk, bread, tins and crisps, and I do eleven or twelve drops a day to corner shops and village stores up the valley. I've only had my licence eighteen months, so the older drivers still give me the easy run, and I still take the hairpin above Millbrook slower than they'd like. What I love is the shopkeepers, like Mrs Petrosyan who saves me a coffee. What wears me out is reversing into tight yards with a queue of cars watching.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And money-wise, how are things at home right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tight, honestly. I live with my partner Dani, who does night shifts as a care worker, and between us we cover the rent and not much else. I've got maybe three hundred in the bank, which is less than a month of anything. Brookfield lost two big shop chains this year, and the newest drivers, which means me, went from five days to four over the winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because everyone's been banging on about robots for years and here we are. At the union meeting I'd say the real fight was always pay and hours, not machines. Online I'd probably not say anything, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my problems stay exactly the same, which isn't great either. I'm still the newest driver on four days a week, still lower pay than the lads who've been there twenty years. Nothing radical changing means nothing gets better on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and try to get back to five days by spring. I'd push the union rep, Gary, to argue that four-day weeks for new starters are just a pay cut with a nicer name. And we'd cut the takeaway on Fridays, that's twenty-five a week we don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about a minute, then the usual knot in my stomach about rent. What scares me isn't robots, it's the winter and the four-day weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the scanner app. What does the bit of AI that does arrive look like in your cab?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd probably make the scanner smarter, tell me the order to do my drops in. I hate that thing already, it freezes on the hill where there's no signal and then I'm stood in the rain waving it about. If it saved Gary in the office ten minutes a day, fine, but I wouldn't touch any of the extra features.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the four-day weeks carried on, which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone bill, because they give you a bit of time. Rent can't go late, the landlord already made a comment last year. Dani would pick up an extra night shift, and I hate that, because then I never see her.

say: Robots were **hype** all along, and the real fight is about **pay and hours**.
I'd tell the **union meeting** that four-day weeks for new starters need sorting first.
think: My problems **stay** the same: newest driver, lower pay, and **four days** a week in winter.
Nothing changing means **nothing gets better** for me on its own.
do: Push **Gary the union rep** to fight four-day weeks for new starters.
Aim to get back to **five days** by spring.
Cut the **Friday takeaway** to save twenty-five a week.
feel: **Brief relief**, then the usual knot about **rent** through the winter.
S0.quote: What scares me isn't robots, it's the winter and the four-day weeks.
fieldNote: Her worry is **already here**: lost contracts cut her to four days before any AI arrives.
She frames everything through **the union** and pay, not technology.
Even small AI features feel like **a nuisance** to her; she says she wouldn't touch them.

steps.text: Keep doing the valley grocery run and ask for five days by spring
Ask the union rep to challenge four-day weeks for new drivers
Stop the Friday takeaway to save twenty-five a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that if the company's saving money with computers, the drivers should see some of it. At the depot I'd be the one asking who's paying for all this. I'd sign whatever petition the union put out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the office goes first and I'm safe for a bit. Nobody's building a robot to carry milk crates down Mrs Petrosyan's steps any time soon. But if the office shrinks, they'll squeeze us harder on times, and I'm already the slow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put, because there's nothing else round here that pays even what Brookfield pays. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a rule that the app can't be used to discipline us. And I'd try to build up a hundred pounds a month in savings, even if it means no holiday this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, like the floor's tilting a bit. I'm not losing my job tomorrow, but I'm the one with the worst times and the least years. When they look for someone to make an example of, it's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the planning software sets your drop times for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's exactly what I'm scared of. A computer doesn't know that the Millbrook shop has a dog loose in the yard and you lose five minutes every time. Twelve drops in a time the computer thinks is fair, and I'd be getting warnings by the second week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. Would that change if the company made you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd use it, I'm not stupid, I need the job. But I'd do the bare minimum and I'd want the union to check what it records about me. I don't want a machine writing my report card.

say: If computers save the company money, **drivers should share** it.
I'd sign any **union petition** about the new software.
think: The **office goes first** and my hands-on work is safe for a while.
Software setting drop times would make me the **slow one** who gets **warnings**.
do: Go to every **union meeting** and push for limits on app discipline.
Try to put away **a hundred pounds** a month and skip the holiday.
Stay at Brookfield because **nothing else nearby** pays as much.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the floor is tilting under her.
Afraid of being **made an example** of as the newest driver.
S1.quote: A computer doesn't know that the Millbrook shop has a dog loose in the yard and you lose five minutes every time.
fieldNote: She sees the **office** going first, but expects the pressure to **land on drivers**.
Her fear is **surveillance and targets**, more than losing the job outright.
She'd use AI **only if forced**, and wants the union to check the data.

steps.text: Ask the union for a rule that the app can't discipline drivers
Save a hundred pounds a month and skip this year's holiday
Stay at Brookfield because no nearby job pays more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, and fast. At work I'd be telling everyone to join the union now, not when the robot trucks turn up. Online I might actually post for once, something about protecting working people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I've got about five years and then I'm done. The thinking stuff goes in 2028, so the office and the route planning, and then by 2031 a robot can drive my truck and carry the crates. I'll be thirty-two with no qualifications except a lorry licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd join every campaign going for a shorter week and a basic income, because I can't fix this on my own. I'd ask Dani about moving to the city where at least there are more jobs, though I'd hate it. I'd probably still drive until they stop me, because I don't know what else I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I worked so hard for that licence, I failed my test twice. Picturing my licence being worthless in five years makes me want to cry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does those three years between the thinking AI and the robots look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably worse pay, because the office is all computer by then and they'll be pushing us to hit times set by a machine. Maybe they keep us on as cheap babysitters until the robots are ready. Three years of being told you're temporary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to the city but you'd hate it. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, really. I'd hate it, but if the choice is the valley with no work or the city with some, I'd go. Dani's job is easier to find anywhere, care work is everywhere, so it'd be my job deciding it.

say: The **government must step in** fast to protect working people.
Everyone at the depot should **join the union** now, before robot trucks arrive.
think: I've got about **five years** before a robot drives my truck.
At thirty-two I'd have **no qualifications** except a lorry licence.
do: Join campaigns for a **shorter week** and a **basic income**.
Talk with Dani about **moving to the city** for more jobs.
Keep **driving until** the company stops her.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of her hard-won licence becoming **worthless**.
S2.quote: I worked so hard for that licence, I failed my test twice. Picturing my licence being worthless in five years makes me want to cry.
fieldNote: She grasps the **three-year gap**: thinking AI hits the office first, then robots take the cab.
She expects the gap years to bring **worse pay** and being treated as temporary.
**Moving** depends on her job, since Dani's care work exists **everywhere**.

steps.text: Join the union campaign for a shorter working week
Vote and campaign for a basic income for laid-off drivers
Plan a move to the city with Dani if valley jobs vanish
Keep driving the Brookfield run until the robots take over

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, really, I'd say we need rules and we need them now. With five years I'd be saying it louder, because there's no excuse for politicians not to plan. I'd tell people at the depot that this time we can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means about eight years before the robots, so I'd be thirty-five. That's a bit more time, but I'm not someone who changes easily, so I'd probably waste half of it hoping it's not true. That's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the union's training committee, if there is one, and push for the company to pay for retraining. Maybe I'd look at the warehouse forklift ticket, because at least it's something. And I'd try to keep the hundred a month in savings going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit ashamed that I know I'd drag my feet. Five years sounds like a lot until you remember how long it took me to pass my driving test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the forklift ticket. Wouldn't robots take the warehouse too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, probably before the trucks, now you say it. I don't know what I'd train for, that's the problem. Nobody in my family has done anything except shops and driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the company to do with those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tell us the truth about the dates, first of all. Then pay for proper training while we're still on full wages, not after they've let us go. Brookfield's owner drives a new car every year, they can afford it.

say: Politicians have **no excuse** not to plan when it's five years away.
I'd tell the depot that this time **we can see** it coming.
think: I'd have about **eight years** before robots take the cab.
I'd probably **waste half the time** hoping it isn't true.
do: Push the company through the union to **pay for retraining**.
Look into a **forklift ticket**, though she doubts it would last.
feel: **Anxious**, and a bit **ashamed** she'd drag her feet.
S3.quote: Five years sounds like a lot until you remember how long it took me to pass my driving test.
fieldNote: She is **honest** about her own **slowness**, which few people admit.
She has **no picture** of what to retrain for; her family knows only shops and driving.
She blames **Brookfield's owner** and wants training paid on **full wages**.

steps.text: Push through the union for company-paid training on full wages
Ask about a forklift licence course at the depot
Keep saving a hundred pounds a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, so no excuses. At the union I'd want a plan for every driver at Brookfield, written down. I'd still say the bosses shouldn't get to keep all the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years plus three for the robots, I'd be about forty when the truck goes. That's half my working life still to go. That's scarier in one way. In the fast one I could say it wasn't my fault. Here I'd have no excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, because I'd still have years of it. But I'd do one course a year, maybe the night classes at the college in town, maths first because I never passed it. And Dani and I would think hard before taking on any car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. It's far enough away that I can breathe, close enough that I know I'd regret doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does forty with no truck look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely can't picture it, which is the problem. Maybe something in care like Dani, robots will take longer to do that, I'd hope. I'd want to still be in the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you wait to see what happens first, or start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My instinct is to wait, I'll be honest. But I'd tell myself to start the maths now, because that's useful whatever happens, and it's free at the college.

say: **Ten years** is enough to do it properly, so **no excuses**.
The union should have a **written plan** for every Brookfield driver.
think: I'd be about **forty** when robots take the truck, with half my working life left.
In the fast one it wasn't my fault; here I'd have **no excuse**.
do: Keep **driving** while doing **one course** a year.
Start the free **maths night class** at the college in town.
Avoid taking on a **car loan** with Dani.
feel: **Able to breathe**, but sure she'd **regret** doing nothing.
S4.quote: With ten years plus three for the robots, I'd be about forty when the truck goes. That's half my working life still to go.
fieldNote: The long warning **shifts blame** onto herself, which she finds uncomfortable.
Her first step is basic: **passing maths**, which she never did at school.
She still wants to stay in **the valley** and wonders about **care work** like Dani.

steps.text: Keep driving the Brookfield run for the next decade
Sign up for the free maths night class at the town college
Hold off on any car loan with Dani

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. I'd be thirty-two with a licence nobody needs and three hundred in the bank. What would help is the union getting a deal now, while we still matter, plus some kind of income for drivers while we retrain, paid by the companies that save the money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about Dani. People forget it's a household. If my job goes and her night shifts are all we've got, that's not a life, that's just surviving.

headlineQuote: I'd be thirty-two with a licence nobody needs and three hundred in the bank.
portrait: Carla is a 27-year-old **junior driver** for a valley grocery wholesaler, with eighteen months behind the wheel.
She lives with Dani, a night-shift **care worker**, and has about **three hundred** saved.
She is **pro-union** and blames bosses who keep the savings, not the machines themselves.
She **resists technology** and admits she'd drag her feet even with years of warning.
Her mood moves from **anxious** about winter hours to **alarmed** by fast AGI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving her at thirty-two with a useless **licence** and almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** struck now, while drivers still matter.
An **income during retraining**, paid by the companies that save the money.
